Five methods: surveys, interviews, participant observation, experiments, analysis of existing data — each with a one-line description, an original example, and one honest limitation
The steps of a study: question, design, data, analyze, report — each named with one line
Samples and representativeness: who you study matters (population vs. sample, random sample)

Honest framing: research is the discipline's reality check

claims.claim: Sociological research is the systematic collection and analysis of evidence about social life; OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e describes sociologists gathering and analyzing empirical evidence from direct experience to understand societies and social interactions.
Empirical evidence is observable and checkable, which is what separates research from intuition, rumor, and personal experience.

A sociological study proceeds through named steps — asking a question, designing the study, collecting data, analyzing data, and reporting results; OpenStax's fuller scientific-method version adds a review of existing sources and hypothesis formulation.

A survey collects data from people who respond to a series of questions about behaviors and opinions; its honest limitation is that it captures what people say they think and do, not necessarily what they really do.

An interview is a one-on-one conversation in which the researcher can ask for clarification; its honest limitation is that it is time-consuming and a researcher who steers or prompts can shape the answers.

Participant observation means joining a group's routine activities to observe them from the inside; its honest limitation is that it is time-consuming, mostly qualitative, and the researcher's presence can change what happens.

Experiments test hypotheses by comparing groups under controlled conditions; their honest limitation is artificiality, including the Hawthorne effect, where people change their behavior because they know they are being studied.

Secondary data analysis studies data already collected by other researchers or agencies (such as the Census Bureau's American Community Survey); its honest limitations are that the data may not fit the exact question and accuracy can be hard to verify.

A study's success depends on how well the sample represents the population; in a random sample, every person in the population has the same chance of being chosen, and a large but unrepresentative sample still misleads.

The American Sociological Association maintains a Code of Ethics requiring sociologists to maintain objectivity and integrity, respect subjects' rights to privacy and dignity, protect subjects from personal harm, preserve confidentiality, and seek informed consent.

Modern research ethics rules grew out of past studies that harmed participants, such as the Tuskegee study, in which men with syphilis were denied treatment so researchers could observe the disease's course.

Every research method has trade-offs; OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e states that every research method comes with plusses and minuses and that the topic of study strongly influences which method is used, which is why strong studies often combine methods.
The American Community Survey is an ongoing yearly survey of U.S. households whose data inform how federal funds are distributed and are used by public officials, planners, and researchers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can sociological research be fully objective, or does every study carry value bias?
positions: Max Weber's value neutrality holds that researchers must keep personal values out of the interpretation and reporting of results (OpenStax 3e, section 2.3).

Many sociologists argue complete objectivity is impossible and caution readers that studies may contain some value bias, so results should be read as one fact-based perspective (OpenStax 3e, section 2.3).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Taught descriptively, as OpenStax frames it: researchers are obligated to report results even when they contradict personal views, while readers should treat any single study as one evidence-based perspective rather than a final verdict. The lesson presents objectivity as an ethical duty and a goal, not a guaranteed outcome.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Should participant observation be overt or covert (participants informed vs. not informed)?
positions: Overt observation respects participants' right to know they are being studied; the Lynds' Middletown study is an example of open field research (OpenStax 3e, section 2.2).

Covert observation can access more authentic behavior, but deception raises ethical problems — the Humphreys study, where a researcher misrepresented his identity, drew ethical criticism (OpenStax 3e, sections 2.2 and 2.3).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the ethics rule as the baseline — informed consent and avoiding harm per the ASA Code of Ethics — and does not endorse covert deception; it notes that choosing an ethical setting or method is the researcher's obligation.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 2.1 Approaches to Sociological Research
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the LibreTexts mirror of the same OpenStax 3e text (socialsci.libretexts.org .../Introductory_Sociology_3e_(OpenStax)/02%3A_Sociological_Research/2.02%3A_Approaches_to_Sociological_Research) because openstax.org blocks direct fetch. Supports: the working definition of sociological research (gathering and analyzing empirical evidence about social life), empirical evidence, the scientific-method steps, and the interpretive framework. The chapter introduction (2.01 on the mirror) provides the reality-check framing: everyday observations carry bias, so sociologists gather and analyze empirical evidence.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 2.2 Research Methods
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the LibreTexts mirror (2.03%3A_Research_Methods on the same book). Supports: surveys (fixed questions; captures what people say, not necessarily what they do), interviews (one-on-one, clarification, risk of steering), participant observation (joining a group's routine activities; time-consuming, qualitative), experiments (control groups, artificiality, Hawthorne effect), secondary data analysis (existing data from agencies like BLS/WHO; fit and verifiability limits), population/sample/random sample definitions, 'every research method comes with plusses and minuses', and the section-summary method table with advantages and challenges per method.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 2.3 Ethical Concerns
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the LibreTexts mirror (2.04%3A_Ethical_Concerns on the same book). Supports: the ASA Code of Ethics requirements (objectivity and integrity, privacy and dignity, protection from harm, confidentiality, informed consent, acknowledging collaboration, disclosing funding), Weber's value neutrality, and the historical unethical studies (Tuskegee, Milgram, Stanford prison experiment, Humphreys, Henrietta Lacks) that motivated modern ethics rules.

sourceRecords.title: ASA Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live (HTTP 200). ASA page states the Code of Ethics 'sets forth the principles and ethical standards that underlie sociologists' scientific and professional responsibilities and conduct' and is administered by the ASA Committee on Professional Ethics. Used to attribute the existence and authority of the ethics code; the specific duties (informed consent, privacy, confidentiality, protection from harm) are summarized per OpenStax 3e section 2.3.
